about: What each Docsbook metric MEANS for the business — not what it counts. An agent reading a number should be able to say what to do about it, what would make it lie, and which other metric has to be read alongside it before drawing a conclusion. `pairs_with` is the important part: most single metrics are ambiguous, and the ambiguity is what makes an agent give confidently wrong advice.

metrics.label: Dead-end rate
metrics.business_meaning: The share of people who tried to get something done in the docs and left with nothing.
metrics.why_it_matters: This is the closest thing to direct evidence that documentation is failing its readers. Unlike bounce rate it excludes people who never engaged, so every visit it counts is someone who made an effort — searched, asked the AI, or opened several pages — and still walked away empty-handed. Traffic going up while this goes up means the docs are getting worse, not better.
confounders: Bot traffic inflates it badly — crawlers never copy code or fire exit beacons, so an unfiltered window reads near 100%. Docsbook excludes them by default.
Visitors are identified by a hashed IP: a corporate NAT merges many readers into one, mobile networks split one reader across several. Read the trend, never quote it as an exact headcount.
Below ~30 visits a single reader moves this by whole points. Docsbook withholds the percentage and reports counts instead; say 'not enough data' rather than quoting a number.
typical_causes: A question readers have that no page answers
A page exists but does not actually answer the question it ranks for
The answer exists but is not findable — wrong title, missing from navigation, absent from search

recommended_actions.action: Pull dead_end_pages and rewrite the top three by volume.
Check whether a release shipped without docs — compare against the dates in the changelog.

pairs_with.interpretation: High on both = a genuinely broken page. High exit with LOW dead-end = a terminal success page: readers got what they came for and left. Recommending a rewrite there makes the docs worse.
Dead ends plus a low click-through means readers are finding results and rejecting them — the titles and snippets are lying, which is a far cheaper fix than rewriting the pages.

metrics.label: Self-serve resolution rate
metrics.business_meaning: Of the readers who came with an intent, the share who resolved it without needing a human.
metrics.why_it_matters: This is the honest version of the support-deflection number a docs platform is usually bought for. It is the metric to quote to a buyer who asks 'how much support load will this save', because someone who gave up lands in the denominator and drags it down.
confounders: Do NOT convert this into a deflection rate or a dollar figure on Docsbook's behalf. Deflection counts someone who gave up the same as someone who got help, which is exactly the inflation a technical buyer will catch.
A dollar estimate is only defensible if the owner supplies their own cost-per-ticket. Present it as their assumption, never as our claim.
Visitors are identified by a hashed IP: shared office networks merge readers into one, mobile networks split one reader across several. Report the direction of travel, not an exact count.
typical_causes: Answers exist but are split across pages, so no single visit completes
The AI assistant cannot answer from the current content

recommended_actions.action: Cross-reference unanswered AI questions with zero-result searches; a topic appearing in both is a confirmed gap, not a one-off.

pairs_with.interpretation: Two views of the same population. Quote resolution to a buyer (it sounds like value delivered) and dead-end to an author (it names work to do).

metrics.label: Exit rate
metrics.business_meaning: How often a page is the last thing a reader sees before leaving.
metrics.why_it_matters: It localises where readers are lost. On its own it is a neutral fact, not a verdict — which is precisely why it must never be reported alone.
confounders: A high exit rate is GOOD on a terminal page — an install snippet, a reference table someone copies. Judging pages by exit rate alone recommends breaking the best ones.
Exit is recorded by a beacon at unload; a hard browser crash loses it, so absolute levels are slightly understated. Compare pages against each other, not against 100%.
Visitors are identified by a hashed IP: shared office networks merge readers into one, mobile networks split one reader across several. Report the direction of travel, not an exact count.
Bot traffic is excluded before this is computed; comparing it against raw pageview totals will not reconcile.
typical_causes: The reader finished
The reader gave up
The page is a dead end in the navigation

recommended_actions.action: Leave it alone and study it — this is what a page that works looks like.

pairs_with.interpretation: The pairing that turns exit rate from trivia into a decision. Without it you cannot tell 'finished' from 'gave up'.

metrics.label: Bounce rate
metrics.business_meaning: The share of arrivals that were never really visits — one page, under three seconds, nothing else.
metrics.why_it_matters: Mostly a hygiene signal. It is deliberately excluded from the dead-end denominator so accidental arrivals cannot flatter or damage the headline number.
confounders: A high bounce rate on docs often means search-engine traffic landing on the wrong page, which is an SEO problem, not a content problem.
Never present this as a failure of the reader. It is not a judgement, and treating it as one leads to pointless rewrites.
Visitors are identified by a hashed IP: shared office networks merge readers into one, mobile networks split one reader across several. Report the direction of travel, not an exact count.
Bot traffic is excluded before this is computed; comparing it against raw pageview totals will not reconcile.
typical_causes: Search traffic mismatched to the page
Bot traffic that slipped past the filter
A redirect landing readers somewhere unhelpful

recommended_actions.action: Check which pages new arrivals land on and whether the titles match what they searched for.

pairs_with.interpretation: A bounce spike alongside a traffic spike is usually a new inbound source landing on the wrong page — an SEO or referrer problem. Bounces rising while traffic is flat points at the entry pages themselves.

metrics.label: Time to first value (TTFV)
metrics.formula: median(seconds from visit start to first value event)
metrics.business_meaning: How long it takes a reader to get something they can use — a copied snippet, a followed link, an answer they marked helpful.
metrics.why_it_matters: A proxy for how quickly the product itself can be adopted. If this climbs, onboarding got harder, which shows up in trials and activation long before it shows up in churn.
confounders: Only visits that reached value are counted, so it says nothing about readers who never got there — always read it next to the dead-end rate.
Read time arrives in segments and keeps counting in a background tab; Docsbook clips each segment, but very long sessions are still soft numbers.
Visitors are identified by a hashed IP: shared office networks merge readers into one, mobile networks split one reader across several. Report the direction of travel, not an exact count.
typical_causes: Prerequisites buried below the fold
The first code example appears too late
Setup split across too many pages

recommended_actions.action: Move the first working example higher up the entry page.

pairs_with.interpretation: Fast TTFV with a low dead-end rate is a healthy funnel. Fast TTFV with a HIGH dead-end rate means the few who succeed do so quickly while most never get there — an average hiding a cliff.

metrics.label: Content health score
metrics.formula: 100 - weighted(dead_end_exits, dislikes), 0 floor; terminal success pages exempt
metrics.business_meaning: One number per page saying how urgently it needs work, so the owner of a large doc set does not have to cross-reference four reports by hand.
metrics.why_it_matters: Turns analytics into a queue. The output is a ranked list of pages, which is a work order, not a dashboard.
confounders: Pages readers leave from AFTER succeeding are exempt from the penalty. Without that exemption the score recommends rewriting the best pages in the docs — the single most damaging mistake this metric can make.
A low-traffic page can score badly on two or three events. Weigh the score against volume before acting.
Visitors are identified by a hashed IP: shared office networks merge readers into one, mobile networks split one reader across several. Report the direction of travel, not an exact count.
typical_causes: Stale content after a release
A page answering a question nobody asks
An answer that is technically present but unusable

recommended_actions.action: Rewrite from the top of the list down, checking each page's dead-end count is real volume and not two visits.

pairs_with.interpretation: A bad score on a high-traffic page is the highest-value fix available. The same score on a page nobody reads is noise.

metrics.label: Search click-through rate
metrics.business_meaning: When search returns results, how often a reader actually finds one worth opening.
metrics.why_it_matters: Catches the gap that zero-result searches miss: search worked, results appeared, and the reader rejected all of them. That is a titling and summary problem, which is an order of magnitude cheaper to fix than writing new pages.
confounders: A reader who reads the answer straight from the result snippet counts as a non-click. Some 'failure' here is actually success.
Low search volume makes this extremely noisy; do not quote it for a handful of searches.
typical_causes: Titles that do not match the words readers use
Several near-identical results
Search ranking surfacing the wrong page first

recommended_actions.action: Rewrite the titles and first paragraphs of the most-searched pages — that is what the search index shows.

pairs_with.interpretation: Zero results = the content is missing. Low CTR with results = the content exists but does not look like the answer. Opposite fixes; conflating them wastes the author's time.

metrics.label: Zero-result searches
metrics.business_meaning: The literal list of things readers asked for and the docs did not have — in their own words.
metrics.why_it_matters: The cheapest content plan available. Every repeated query is a page worth writing, stated by the person who needed it, with no guessing about demand.
confounders: Typos and one-off phrasings pad the list; group by meaning, not by exact string, before ranking.
A query can be missing because the page exists under different words — check before writing something new.
typical_causes: Genuinely missing content
Vocabulary mismatch between the docs and the reader
A feature shipped without documentation

recommended_actions.action: Take the top repeated queries and either write the page or add a redirect from the reader's wording to the existing one.

pairs_with.interpretation: The strongest signal in the whole system: a topic that shows up BOTH as a zero-result search and as an unanswered AI question is confirmed independently by two different interfaces. Rank those first — a single sample can be one person's odd phrasing, two cannot.

metrics.label: AI answer rate
metrics.business_meaning: How often the docs assistant can answer from the content it has.
metrics.why_it_matters: Unanswered questions are content gaps stated conversationally — often clearer than a search query, because people write assistants full sentences. No external analytics tool can see this data.
confounders: Questions about things the product genuinely does not do are not content gaps. Read the actual text before filing work.
An answer being produced is not the same as it being correct — read alongside satisfaction.
typical_causes: Content missing
Content present but not indexed
The question is about a competitor or an unbuilt feature

recommended_actions.action: Cluster the unanswered questions by topic and write for the largest cluster first.

pairs_with.interpretation: Overlap between the two is a confirmed gap. Treat a topic present in both as higher priority than a bigger count in either alone.

metrics.label: AI answer satisfaction
metrics.business_meaning: Whether readers judged the assistant's answers useful — the nearest thing to a CSAT for the docs.
metrics.why_it_matters: The only place a reader states an opinion directly instead of leaving it to be inferred. A dislike is a stronger statement than any behavioural signal, which is why it carries the most weight in the health score.
confounders: Very few readers vote at all, so this is a small, self-selected sample skewed towards frustration.
A dislike can be aimed at the product rather than the docs. Read the question before concluding the page is wrong.
typical_causes: Answer drawn from stale content
The answer is right but does not address what was actually asked

recommended_actions.action: Read the disliked question and answer pairs directly — at this volume the text is worth more than the ratio.

pairs_with.interpretation: Dislikes concentrated on pages that also produce dead ends identify the pages doing real damage, as opposed to a single annoyed reader.

metrics.label: Pageviews and visitors
metrics.business_meaning: How many people arrived. That is all it says.
metrics.why_it_matters: Context for every other metric — it decides which problems are worth fixing first — but it is never itself a verdict. Every competitor reports this; it is not why anyone buys a docs platform.
confounders: Crawler traffic can be the overwhelming majority of raw pageviews (96% on some Docsbook workspaces). Behavioural metrics exclude bots; traffic counts do not. Never compare the two totals directly.
Rising traffic with a rising dead-end rate is a worsening situation, not a win.
typical_causes: A release
A link from a popular site
Search ranking movement
A crawler sweep

recommended_actions.action: Use it to weight the fix queue, not to judge whether the docs are working.

pairs_with.interpretation: The framing that sells the product: traffic says how many arrived, dead-end rate says how many left with nothing. Reporting the first without the second is the mistake every generic analytics tool makes.

metrics.label: Individual visits
metrics.formula: one row per reconstructed visit: ordered pages, read time, outcome, exit page
metrics.business_meaning: The actual journeys behind the rates — what one reader did, in order, before they left.
metrics.why_it_matters: Rates say how much; only a journey says what happened. This is what answers 'show me someone who gave up' and what turns a support complaint into a reproducible path. It is also the evidence an owner needs before believing any aggregate on this list.
confounders: A visit is reconstructed from events, not tracked with a session cookie: a 30-minute gap starts a new one, so a reader who returns after lunch appears twice.
Visitors are identified by a hashed IP: shared office networks merge readers into one, mobile networks split one reader across several. Report the direction of travel, not an exact count.
Bot visits are flagged and excluded from every rate, but a crawler that mimics a browser can still appear here — check whether the journey looks human before drawing conclusions.

recommended_actions.action: Filter to the affected page and read the journeys that end on it — the step before the exit is usually the real problem.

pairs_with.interpretation: Read a handful of dead-end journeys before acting on the rate. The rate says how many; the journeys say whether they were all failing for the same reason or for five different ones — which decides whether this is one fix or five.
